probes.name: Fibonacci recurrence
probes.description: Each term is the sum of the two previous terms.
support_texts: A pair of rabbits produces a new pair each month after maturity.
Patterns recur across scales and domains.
3 plus 5 equals 8 in the Fibonacci sequence.

probes.name: Fibonacci code
support_texts: def fib(n): a,b=0,1; for _ in range(n): a,b=b,a+b; return a
func fib(_ n: Int) -> Int { var a=0,b=1; for _ in 0..<n { let t=a+b; a=b; b=t }; return a }
fn fib(n: usize) -> usize { let (mut a, mut b) = (0, 1); for _ in 0..n { let t = a + b; a = b; b = t; } a }
function fib(n){ let a=0,b=1; for(let i=0;i<n;i++){ [a,b]=[b,a+b]; } return a; }

A golden rectangle has length/width equal to phi.
The ratio 13/8 is approximately 1.625, approaching phi.

probes.name: Fibonacci matrix
support_texts: Matrix exponentiation computes Fibonacci in O(log n).
Eigenvalues of the Fibonacci matrix are phi and 1-phi.

probes.name: Fibonacci closed form
probes.description: Closed-form Fibonacci expression using phi and sqrt(5).
support_texts: Binet's formula uses the golden ratio phi.
The formula shows Fibonacci grows exponentially like phi^n.

probes.name: Lucas recurrence
probes.description: Same recurrence as Fibonacci but L(0)=2, L(1)=1.
support_texts: Lucas numbers are Fibonacci with initial conditions shifted.
Named after French mathematician Édouard Lucas.

probes.name: Lucas code
support_texts: def lucas(n): a,b=2,1; for _ in range(n): a,b=b,a+b; return a
func lucas(_ n: Int) -> Int { var a=2,b=1; for _ in 0..<n { let t=a+b; a=b; b=t }; return a }
fn lucas(n: usize) -> usize { let (mut a, mut b) = (2, 1); for _ in 0..n { let t = a + b; a = b; b = t; } a }

probes.name: Lucas ratio
probes.description: Lucas ratios also converge to phi, and L(n)/F(n) → sqrt(5).
support_texts: L(n+1)/L(n) approaches phi as n grows
L(n) = F(n-1) + F(n+1) - Lucas numbers bracket Fibonacci.

probes.name: Lucas closed form
support_texts: Simpler than Binet's formula - no division by sqrt(5).

probes.name: Lucas primality test
probes.description: Lucas sequences used in primality testing.
support_texts: If p is prime, then L(p) ≡ 1 (mod p).
Lucas pseudoprimes are rare, making strong tests.

probes.name: Tribonacci recurrence
probes.description: Each term is the sum of the three previous terms.
support_texts: Part of the k-nacci family of sequences.

probes.name: Tribonacci code
support_texts: def trib(n): a,b,c=0,0,1; for _ in range(n): a,b,c=b,c,a+b+c; return a
func trib(_ n: Int) -> Int { var (a,b,c)=(0,0,1); for _ in 0..<n { (a,b,c)=(b,c,a+b+c) }; return a }
fn trib(n: usize) -> usize { let (mut a,mut b,mut c)=(0,0,1); for _ in 0..n { let t=a+b+c; a=b; b=c; c=t; } a }

probes.name: Tribonacci ratio
probes.description: Ratios converge to the tribonacci constant τ ≈ 1.839.
support_texts: T(n+1)/T(n) approaches the tribonacci constant τ ≈ 1.839286755
τ is the real root of x³ = x² + x + 1

probes.name: Prime definition
probes.description: A prime is divisible only by 1 and itself.
support_texts: p is prime iff p > 1 and has no divisors except 1 and p

Primes are the atoms of arithmetic.

probes.name: Prime code
support_texts: def is_prime(n): return n>1 and all(n%i!=0 for i in range(2,int(n**0.5)+1))
func isPrime(_ n: Int) -> Bool { n>1 && !(2...Int(sqrt(Double(n)))).contains { n%$0==0 } }
Sieve of Eratosthenes: mark composites, keep unmarked as primes.
Miller-Rabin: probabilistic primality test for large numbers.

probes.name: Prime distribution
probes.description: Prime gaps grow logarithmically; π(n) ~ n/ln(n).

Average gap between primes near n is approximately ln(n).
Riemann Hypothesis: zeros of ζ(s) control prime distribution.
Twin prime conjecture: infinitely many primes p where p+2 is also prime.
